question: What does self-medication mean in everyday healthcare?

options.A: Receiving free drug samples directly from a licensed hospital pharmacist
options.B: Sharing prescribed drugs strictly among family members living in the same house
options.C: Taking medications without a prescription from a qualified practitioner
options.D: Buying herbal teas from registered supermarkets for general wellness

explanation: Spot on! Self-medication simply means taking drugs without getting professional guidance or a valid prescription first. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is self-medication so common across Nigeria?

options.A: Standard hospitals rarely stock basic pain relief tablets
options.B: People prefer reading package leaflets over talking to doctors
options.C: Hospital queues, costs, and easy access to open-air drug markets drive the practice
options.D: The government mandates that every citizen treat themselves first

explanation: You got it! Long wait times at clinics and financial constraints often push people to easily accessible informal drug vendors instead. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which group of drugs is most commonly grabbed off the shelf for everyday aches without a prescription?
explanation: That's right! Pain relievers like ibuprofen (NSADs) are easy to buy over the counter, making them hot targets for misuse when body pains flare up. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h2)

question: A patient says they drink strong cough syrup containing codeine every day just to chill and relax. What is happening here?

options.A: Proper management of a chronic upper respiratory infection
options.B: Substance misuse and potential psychological dependence
options.C: An effective strategy to build natural immunity against colds
options.D: A harmless alternative to sleeping pills

explanation: Well done! Using codeine-lacking syrups just for a high or relaxation leads straight down the road to substance abuse and addiction. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which two major organs work the hardest to process all those self-prescribed drugs?
explanation: Spot on! The liver breaks down drugs while the kidneys filter them out, putting them right in the firing line for toxicity when we misuse medications. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h3)

question: Someone has been swallowing heavy doses of strong painkillers daily for months and now has severe belly pain and dark, tarry stools. What's the likely culprit?

options.A: A normal side effect that will disappear without intervention
options.B: An acute respiratory infection affecting the lower gut
options.C: Severe dehydration from drinking too much cold water
options.D: Gastrointestinal bleeding caused by drug erosion of the stomach lining

explanation: You nailed it! Unchecked painkillers irritate and eat away at the stomach lining, causing bleeding that turns stools dark and tarry. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h3)

question: Why does stopping your antibiotics halfway through cause drug resistance?

options.A: It forces the body to produce too many white blood cells
options.B: It makes the remaining tablets expire much faster in storage
options.C: It allows the strongest bacteria to survive, mutate, and multiply
options.D: It immediately cures the viral infection causing the fever

explanation: Exactly! Stopping early kills only the weak germs, leaving the tough, stubborn bacteria alive to multiply and become resistant to future drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a good reason to avoid using leftover antibiotics for a new cold?

options.A: Colds are usually caused by viruses, which antibiotics cannot kill
options.B: Using leftover drugs can lead to incorrect dosing and drug resistance
options.C: Leftover antibiotics are guaranteed to work faster than fresh prescriptions
options.D: Sharing drugs promotes dangerous resistance patterns in the community

explanation: That's right! Leftover drugs are never a magic shortcut; using them wrongly for viral colds is useless and dangerous. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h4)

question: What happens when someone mixes sleeping pills (sedatives) with alcohol?

options.A: Immediate neutralization of all toxic chemicals in the blood
options.B: A sudden increase in physical stamina and alertness
options.C: Severe respiratory suppression and potential breathing failure
options.D: Enhanced absorption of vital nutrients in the stomach

explanation: Spot on! Both alcohol and sedatives slow down the brain. Combining them can make breathing slow down to a dangerous, fatal stop. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why is mixing local herbal mixtures with modern hospital drugs a hidden danger during self-medication?

options.A: Herbal mixtures are always chemically identical to factory-made pills
options.B: Herbs always taste too bitter to swallow with tablets
options.C: Unregulated herbs may contain hidden drugs that cause harmful interactions
options.D: Modern drugs completely destroy the healing power of leaves

explanation: You got it! Local mixtures often have active chemical ingredients that clash unpredictably with your hospital prescription. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the main body purpose of warning signs like pain and fever?

options.A: To act as warning signals indicating internal distress or disease
options.B: To punish the patient for eating unhealthy foods
options.C: To slow down normal blood circulation in the limbs
options.D: To increase the body weight of an infected person

explanation: Exactly! Think of pain and fever as the body's alarm system alerting you that something inside needs attention. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h6)

question: A patient takes strong painkillers daily for tummy cramps instead of seeing a doctor. What is the major danger here?

options.A: The abdominal muscles will become permanently paralyzed
options.B: The underlying disease, such as appendicitis, goes undiagnosed until it worsens
options.C: The body will stop producing natural digestive enzymes
options.D: The patient will develop an instant allergy to all known antibiotics

explanation: Well done! Masking the pain with drugs doesn't cure the problem; it just keeps you quiet while a serious condition gets worse. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why are babies and young children extra vulnerable to the risks of self-medication?

options.A: They refuse to swallow any medication unless it is sweet
options.B: Their liver and kidney enzyme systems are still immature
options.C: Their skin absorbs chemical substances much slower than adults
options.D: They have higher blood volume than healthy adults

explanation: Spot on! Children's bodies process drugs differently because their organs aren't fully developed yet to clear toxins easily. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why must pregnant women avoid self-medication at all costs?

options.A: Pregnancy completely stops the stomach from absorbing pills
options.B: Drugs can cross the placenta and harm the developing foetus
options.C: Pregnant women are immune to all standard pain relievers
options.D: Unprescribed drugs only affect the mother's hair growth

explanation: You nailed it! Many drugs can slip across the placenta barrier and interfere with the safe growth of the unborn baby. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h7)

question: As a nurse, what is a key duty when taking a patient's medication history?

options.A: Prescribing new antibiotics if the patient feels weak
options.B: Asking specifically about self-prescribed drugs, herbs, and leftover pills
options.C: Telling the patient to stop asking questions about their treatment
options.D: Selling safe over-the-counter drugs directly from the nursing station

explanation: That's right! Always dig deeper during assessments to find out what informal remedies or leftover pills the patient has taken. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h8)

question: A patient says they want to save half their leftover antibiotics for a family member who might fall sick later. How should you respond?

options.A: Explain the dangers of sharing medications and encourage proper disposal
options.B: Write down instructions on which family member should take the leftover pills
options.C: Advise the patient to double the dose next time someone coughs
options.D: Praise the patient for being resourceful and saving money

explanation: Wonderful! As a nurse, you want to warmly educate patients on why sharing drugs spreads resistance and toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T4#GNS215_U4_T4_h8)
